prompt: A messaging app stores 40 TB of messages and grows 2 TB a month. A single database server can no longer hold it.
why: More data than one machine can hold: partition by a key (such as conversation ID) across shards.
trap: Replicas copy all of the data, so every replica is still 40 TB.

prompt: A metrics service ingests 500k writes per second, and the primary database's CPU is pinned, even though reads are rare.
why: Limited by write throughput: split the writes across shards so each primary takes a slice.
trap: Replicas and caches help reads. Every write still lands on a single primary.

prompt: A SaaS product has 30,000 customer companies. Queries never cross companies, and the largest customers are slowing down everyone else.
why: The tenant is a natural shard key. The biggest tenants can each get their own shard.
trap: Rate limiting would throttle the customers you most want to keep happy.

prompt: A ride app's trips are always between riders and drivers in the same city, and the trips table has billions of rows.
why: Shard by city or region so each query stays on one shard.
trap: A CDN puts static files near users. It doesn't store trip records.

prompt: Users are split across servers by the first letter of their username, and the 'S' server is overloaded while 'X' sits idle.
why: The shard key is bad. Reshard by a hash of the user ID (ideally with consistent hashing) to spread users evenly.
trap: It's still a sharding problem. Fix the key instead of adding band-aids.

prompt: A URL shortener stores 10 billion short codes, and the lookup index no longer fits in one machine's memory.
tells: no longer fits in one machine's memory
why: Partition by a hash of the code so each shard holds one slice of the index.
trap: A cache helps popular links, but the full index still has to live somewhere.

prompt: A chat service keeps each conversation's history together, and almost every query reads one conversation. The single database has hit its write limit.
tells: almost every query reads one conversation
why: Use the conversation ID as the shard key: every query hits one shard, and writes spread across all of them.
trap: A queue smooths out bursts, but a steady write volume needs more write capacity.

prompt: IoT sensors write readings forever. Queries almost always ask about one device over a time range, and the table is growing past what one node can store.
tells: one device over a time range
past what one node can store
why: Partition by device (and then by time) so each query touches a single shard.
trap: A queue helps with ingestion bursts, not with running out of storage.

prompt: An IoT platform writes 500,000 rows per second, far more than one database server can accept.
tells: more than one database server can accept
why: Split writes across servers by device ID.
trap: Replicas copy every write to every node, so they add read capacity, not write capacity.

prompt: A SaaS database has grown to 40 TB. Nearly every query filters by customer_id.
tells: Nearly every query filters by customer_id
why: customer_id is a natural shard key: each query hits one shard.
trap: Replicas copy all 40 TB to each node, which doesn't solve the size problem.

prompt: A URL shortener stores 20 billion short codes, and lookups are always by the exact code.
why: Hash the code to pick a shard; each lookup touches one machine.
trap: Consistent hashing is a way to shard, but the core need is splitting data across machines.
